Two methodologies, one chain. Culvert and debris-flow risk screening runs on two complementary engines. CULVERT (culvert-at-risk.org, USDA Forest Service / FHWA) screens every road-stream crossing for four hazards - flood overtopping, upland erosion (WEPP/RUSLE), debris flow (WDFM), bank erosion (SBEVA) - into one EHVI score. USGS WildCat covers the post-fire debris-flow case (likelihood and volume from soil burn severity), which TRPA runs in-house. This page supplies the trigger climatology both need; WEPP/WEPPcloud hindcasts validate them against real failures like July 14.

Getting started with the current culvert layer

The map's Culverts toggle carries all 7,858 compiled crossings with condition where it exists.i Toggle it with WEPP sediment and burst hotspots to find crossings under both high sediment supply and repeat storm cores.i

Data governance. This embedded layer contains no NDOT records (county, Caltrans, and TRPA legacy sources only), so it is clean for CULVERT upload. If NDOT state-highway culverts are added later, they are TRPA-only under the sharing agreement - do not upload NDOT-derived data to CULVERT or any third-party service without NDOT sign-off.
The hazard-layer build. Debris flow is the one selected PROTECT hazard with no existing basin-wide layer. USGS WildCat (the operational post-fire debris-flow tool, v1.1.1 verified) fills it from the debris-flow/ pipeline: for each road segment, culvert, and bridge, the modeled probability, volume, and hazard class of a post-fire debris flow reaching it. This tab is the working plan; the trigger storms live on the other tabs of this page.

Why WildCat: it is the USGS operational standard behind their post-fire hazard portal, it supports pre-fire planning through constant burn-severity inputs, every command writes a config record that exactly reproduces its outputs, and it slots between WEPP (chronic erosion) and site-scale runout modeling as the network-scale screening layer.

The plan, six stages

1. Stand up the dedicated wildcat conda environment (rasterio/fiona cannot share arcpy's GDAL). 2. Acquire the static inputs once, USGS 3DEP 10 m DEM (the models are calibrated at 10 m, finer lidar is deliberately not used), STATSGO KF-factors, LANDFIRE EVT. 3. Validate on the Caldor Fire 2021 with real perimeter and dNBR against the published USGS assessment. 4. Run the pre-fire planning scenario, hypothetical moderate burn over HUC12 watersheds intersecting the highway corridors. 5. Apply Tahoe design storms from Atlas 14 (31.6 / 49.6 / 63.8 mm/hr I15 for 2-, 10-, 25-yr basin medians), then repeat with climate-scaled intensities. 6. Intersect exported segments and basins with roads, culverts, and bridges to produce the debris-flow Exposure inputs for the index. Target, a reviewed layer for Workshop 1 in Nov 2026.

15-minute design storms for the M1 model

Atlas 14 partial-duration 15-minute intensities at the eight basin points (basin median in navy, USGS default assessment intensities dashed). Even the basin's 2-yr storm (31.6 mm/hr) exceeds three of the four USGS defaults, so Tahoe-specific design storms are required, the defaults would materially understate likelihoods.

Source and processing

Hourly precipitation is NOAA MRMS MultiSensor QPE (1-hour, Pass 2) - radar-based quantitative precipitation estimates corrected with gauges and model data, on a ~1 km grid, retrieved from the Iowa State mtarchive. Each event is a 72-hour window clipped to the basin bounding box (−120.5..−119.5, 38.5..39.5). Exceedance scoring compares event running-maximum depths (1-hr, 6-hr, 24-hr) at the cell nearest each of eight NOAA Atlas 14 points against that point's partial-duration-series frequency estimates.

Debris-flow connection

These storms are the trigger side of the basin's landslide / debris flow problem (pairs LS-C and LS-R in the Task 3 hazard-asset matrix, with FL-C and FL-R sharing the same storm inputs). The storm structure shown here - short-duration convective rates versus long-duration saturation - is exactly what distinguishes the candidate climate trigger metrics (max 1-day, max 3-day, max 60-day, P99) under review with ICF, and provides the design-storm input for the response models: WEPP Cloud hillslope erosion, USGS WildCat post-fire debris flow (running at TRPA), and HEC-HMS post-wildfire parameterization per the ICF VA deck.

Screening methodologies, CULVERT and WildCat

Crossing-scale risk runs on the CULVERT tool (USDA Forest Service / FHWA / U. North Georgia / U. Idaho): watershed delineation from USGS DEMs, hydrologic vulnerability (regional frequency analysis, TR-55/TR-20, Rational Method against NOAA Atlas 14 design storms), and hydrogeomorphic vulnerability (WEPP + RUSLE upland loading, WDFM debris flow, SBEVA bank erosion) ensembled into an EHVI score per crossing. USGS WildCat provides the post-fire debris-flow complement (likelihood and volume from soil burn severity), run in-house at TRPA. CULVERT's design storms are stationary Atlas 14 - the storm-frequency work on this page (WRF change factors, Atlas 15 tracking) is the future-conditions layer applied on top, and the July 14 hindcast is the local validation case. TRPA is collaborating directly with the CULVERT developer.

Frequency and consequence pipeline

The Storm Frequency tab chains three analyses. Observed frequency comes from a catalog of screened days (gridMET daily max-cell ≥18 mm in summer plus the largest all-season days) scanned in MRMS hourly data for cell-hours over Atlas 14 1-hr depths - seven distinct ≥10-yr-burst episodes in five years. Future scaling comes from UCLA WRF hourly precipitation on the 3 km inner domain (store cadcat/wrf/ucla, 1hr/prec, d03; the climate pipeline's wind pulls use the coarser 9 km d02 grid), models EC-Earth3 + MIROC6, SSP3-7.0. The WRF change factors here are provisional and follow the same human review gate as the climate explorer's published projections; treat them as draft until that review is logged in the climate CHANGELOG. Continuing the chain: by 2070–2099 the basin's annual max 1-hr rate rises ~37 percent and hours over the 10-yr threshold multiply ~4.6×, implying several such episodes per year late century. The July 14 debris flow itself is hindcast at its mapped location (39.12675, −120.24278): the site received a sub-2-yr storm, and WEPP shows zero response on an intact slope versus an erosive response on a disturbed one - evidence that the LS pairs need slope susceptibility crossed with moderate-storm frequency, not extreme-storm frequency alone. Each cataloged burst is also run through WEPP as a single-storm event parameterized from its observed depth, duration, and peak rate - connecting every precipitation anomaly directly to a hillslope sediment response, observed and future-intensified. Longer-term consequences are demonstrated with 30-year WEPP runs (Tahoe City CLIGEN climate, CAGWIN soil, BAER burn treatments): high-severity fire raises sediment yield ~370× over unburned, and the future-scaled climate adds ~34 percent on top of the burned case - fire and intensifying storms compound. Production consequence runs should go through WEPPcloud on real delineated hillslopes with SSURGO soils.

Caveats

The MRMS MultiSensor product archive begins in late 2020, so observed frequency rests on about five years - treat the per-year rate as approximate. The burst catalog only scans screened candidate days, so it is a lower bound. WEPP demo numbers use one synthetic hillslope and simplified burn adjustments. Radar QPE in complex terrain can under-detect shallow orographic precipitation and overshoot in beam-blocked valleys; treat cell-scale values as estimates, strongest for convective events like this one. Atlas 14 is stationary (no climate adjustment) and its point estimates are compared against ~1 km cells, not gauges. The MRMS archive begins in late 2014; earlier events need Stage IV or gridMET daily reconstruction. Companion page: the Climate Data Explorer covers the projection side of the same story. Internal review draft; do not circulate outside the project team.
